La disponibilité des aliments de différe: Availability of foods from different cultures at food banks
« Nous essayons de répondre aux demandes: “We try to meet the demands of the different communities.”
En ce dernier jour de novembre, aux alen: On the last day of November, around 2 p.m., Mohamed* stands in front of the Milano grocery store in Little Italy. Shyly, he approaches with a modest request: “Salam, could you help me?” he murmurs, holding out a scrap of paper, eyes lowered.
Sur ce morceau de papier froissé se trou: On the crumpled piece of paper is a list of basic groceries: basmati rice, milk, eggs, garam masala, onions, peppers, flour and meat.
En se dirigeant vers une banque alimenta: As he heads toward a nearby food bank, he points out: “But over there, they have no rice and no halal meat.”
Le récit de Mohamed n’est malheureusemen: Mohamed’s story, unfortunately, is not unique. According to the Hunger Count 2023, nearly a quarter of food bank users are newcomers with various statuses: asylum seekers, refugees, and permanent or temporary immigrants.
La Converse s’est penchée sur la disponi: La Converse looked into the availability of products from different culinary traditions at food banks, and into lower-cost alternatives.
Le vendredi 8 décembre vers 14 h, le Cen: On Friday, December 8, around 2 p.m., the Centre d’entraide aux familles (CEAF) in Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles is getting ready for the opening of its weekly food counter in an hour. Despite the cold, a dozen people are already waiting outside.
La directrice, Yolette Café, nous accuei: The director, Yolette Café, welcomes us with a smile, her winter coat zipped all the way up: “As you can see, the vast majority of the people we serve are from immigrant backgrounds, and the food we receive doesn’t reflect their culinary diversity. But I can’t go looking for specific foods when I’m not even sure we’ll have basic staples.”
À l’intérieur, la pièce est divisée grâc: Inside, the room is divided by partitions. On one side, about thirty chairs are carefully arranged, creating a welcoming space. On the other, the meticulous preparation of food baskets and boxes is under way. The volunteers have formed two teams. The most agile are unloading the truck filled with cartons of food and carrying them carefully to the reception room.
La directrice place des concombres dans: The director places cucumbers in boxes: “We help three main groups: newcomers—especially asylum seekers—the new poor, and seniors.”
« Veillez à ce qu’il reste suffisamment: “Make sure there’s enough food left to prepare emergency boxes,” Yolette reminds the volunteers, in a voice both strong and gentle, as they set the finished boxes on the floor.
Cette semaine, on trouve dans le panier: This week, the CEAF weekly basket contains a few fruits and vegetables, chicken strips, a can of tuna, a box of juice, Cheerios cereal, instant coffee, a litre of 2% milk, chips, sandwich bread, a beer, yogurt and slices of banana bread.
« Nous recevons des livraisons de viande: “We receive meat deliveries twice a month, and today is distribution day. Unfortunately, halal meat is rarely included, which means our Muslim clientele can’t benefit from this offering,” Yolette explains.

Les portes du centre s’ouvrent dans une: The centre’s doors open in about fifteen minutes, but a few people who came to register for the Christmas basket, which will be distributed on the 19th, are let in early. The volunteer team greets them and offers them hot coffee.
Ils parlent entre eux en créole et évoqu: They speak among themselves in Creole and talk about the recipes they’ll try to make for the holidays if they receive the right ingredients, such as sweet potatoes, squash, plantains, and red and black beans.
Tout en les écoutant, Yolette nous expli: As she listens to them, Yolette explains: “To prepare these recipes, we often lack ingredients, because the food we receive doesn’t necessarily match their culinary traditions. We have no power to select the items that end up in our baskets; it’s Moisson Montréal that sends them to us.”
Contactée à cet effet, la responsable de: Contacted about this, Moisson Montréal’s procurement manager, Lissa Huneault, told us that “since we [Moisson Montréal] accept donations, I depend on what I receive, but I really do make an effort to get as much food as possible that will appeal to all communities.”
Par exemple, l’organisme a mis « du riz: For example, the organization put “rice in the Christmas boxes, knowing that this ingredient is culturally accepted by everyone and is also necessary in many cultures.”
« Effectivement, on y trouve du riz », c: “Indeed, there’s rice,” Yolette notes as she opens one of the Moisson Montréal boxes. “Haitians, Syrians and Pakistanis, for example, eat a lot of rice, but the 700 g bag that Moisson included isn’t going to be enough for a family with teenagers,” she says.
Elle poursuit en énumérant les produits: She goes on listing the products: “They also added instant noodles, Chocomax, a box of juice, cookies, a package of macaroni and canned goods, but unfortunately, no vegetables, no fruit and no dairy products. My goal is to include at least three complete meals per basket.
Un peu déçue, la directrice avoue : « No: A little disappointed, the director admits: “We have about 200 Christmas baskets to prepare and we have to buy items to fill them out. We wanted to give people turkey or chicken, but where are we going to find the money?”
À ce sujet, elle interpelle sa collègue,: On that point, she calls over her colleague, Caroline Audain, who volunteers to raise funds. “Our clients struggle all year long, but they love to get together over a good meal during the holidays, and it’s going to be hard to make ends meet this year,” laments Caroline, a real estate broker by profession.
« Cette semaine, je me suis rendue dans: “This week, I went to a grocery store to buy more rice, different kinds of beans and potatoes for our clientele, many of whom are of Haitian origin. They celebrate Christmas, New Year’s Day and a national holiday during this period,” Yolette continues.
« C’est important d’avoir des gens qui d: “It’s important to have people deciding on the supplies for the communities they serve, because they understand how important it is to come together over a good meal,” says Caroline.
Étant issue de l’immigration haïtienne,: Being of Haitian immigrant background herself, she believes it’s a necessary effort, because “food is also a way to feel at home.”

Il est 15 h, les portes du centre sont o: It’s 3 p.m., and the centre’s doors are open to users. Within a few minutes, the room is packed, and the line outside is just as long, despite the cold.
Parmi les premiers bénéficiaires du pani: Among the first recipients of the weekly basket is Salma*. “I’ve been in Quebec for 18 years, but this year is the first time I’ve gone to a food bank. I had to stop working six years ago because of an operation, and my family and I were living on my husband’s salary. Everything was fine, but this year has been very hard, we can’t keep up.”
D’origine syrienne, Salma explique que s: Originally from Syria, Salma explains that her children don’t know their family is among the thousands of Quebecers who depend on food aid to meet their needs. “I don’t really have a choice anymore if I want to cut expenses with this unbearable inflation.”
Par le biais de le CEAF, Salma et sa fam: Through the CEAF, Salma and her family have discovered many new products. “For example, I had never cooked with plantain before this year. People here are kind, they explain to us how to do it,” she says, referring to the staff and the other users.
En l’écoutant, Rania*, une maman algérie: Listening to her, Rania*, an Algerian mother of three teenagers, joins the conversation to add: “You know what I’d really like to eat? Figs from back home. But they’re really expensive. It would be so nice if they brought some in one day.”
Les deux femmes, presque à l’unisson, di: The two women, almost in unison, say they want halal meat. “Honestly, we don’t buy it very often,” says Rania. “When we do buy it, it’s not to eat it as a meal, but to flavour our dishes.”
Puis, avançant dans la file, Laury*, une: Then, moving forward in the line, Laury*, a newly arrived Haitian, stops to greet Salma and Rania.
« Moi, j’habite à Montréal-Nord, mais je: “I live in Montréal-Nord, but I come all the way here because I know they try to hand out food from back home. That’s not the case at the food banks near me. Here, the team working looks like us. I can vouch for their generosity of spirit. They never turn anyone away. They always find a way to give something,” she tells us before heading into the reception room.
Il est 15 h 45, la file s’étire toujours: It’s 3:45 p.m., the line is still stretching on, and the CEAF is buzzing with the conversations of users, some seated, but most standing. Volunteers keep putting together weekly baskets and handing them out to clients. Yolette asks for everyone’s attention: “We’re holding a Christmas meal on the 29th, and there will be turkey! Come, we want to see you, we want to get to know you, we never have time to really talk.”
L’annonce terminée, les gens applaudisse: When the announcement is over, people applaud, some promise to come, and the hubbub starts up again in full force.
Kathleen Phaëton, Yitong Cheng et Mame B: Kathleen Phaëton, Yitong Cheng and Mame Bigué Dieng of the Carrefour Populaire de Saint-Michel. Photo: Katharine Norva
Toujours dans l’est de la ville, au Carr: Still in the east end of the city, at the Carrefour Populaire de Saint-Michel, the demand for food aid is also high.
Dans la cuisine communautaire du Carrefo: In the Carrefour’s community kitchen, the team of staff members and volunteers gathers around the table, ready to share a meal. On today’s menu: spaghetti with halal meat, prepared by the cook who oversees the community meals.
La coordonnatrice, Mame Bigué Dieng, men: The coordinator, Mame Bigué Dieng, mentions that food is still missing to complete the Christmas boxes. She explains that she also buys supplies <l1>to diversify the products</l1> offered to recipients, such as halal meat.
« Ce qui est bien ici, c’est qu’on a Ma: “What’s great here is that we have Ma boîte à provisions, which lets us get better prices and look for products that reflect our clientele. Look, we’re cooking with halal meat for our volunteers.”
« Par exemple, durant l’Aïd, on achète d: “For example, during Eid, we buy halal meat for Muslims and medium-grain couscous that suits North African culinary habits,” the coordinator points out.
<strong>Ma boîte à provisions : un march: Ma boîte à provisions: a market for everyone
Plus de bénévoles se joignent à la tablé: More volunteers join the table; they have just finished putting together the Ma boîte à provisions baskets.
En 2011, un groupe de résidents engagés: In 2011, a group of engaged Saint-Michel residents joined forces to put an innovative idea into practice: “By buying in larger quantities, by doing our shopping together, maybe we could lower the cost of our groceries.”
Plus d’une décennie plus tard, ce groupe: More than a decade later, that buying group has become Ma boîte à provisions. “At the beginning, we had about ten products from a single supplier. Now we offer nearly 400 items distributed by a variety of different suppliers,” says Yitong Chen, the development officer for Ma boîte à provisions.
Désormais, Ma Boîte à provisions propose: Ma boîte à provisions now offers, every two weeks, an affordable selection of fresh, varied, local foods. Free delivery is even available in the neighbourhood for seniors and people with reduced mobility.
« Malheureusement, pour l’instant, nous: “Unfortunately, for now, we can’t extend delivery to everyone, because our delivery person is also the caretaker, and we’re trying to lighten his responsibilities. However, since we’re a community market, everyone is welcome to place an order with us and benefit from our good prices; it’s not only for neighbourhood residents,” she says.
« Le quartier Saint-Michel est très mult: “The Saint-Michel neighbourhood is very multicultural, attracting users from many backgrounds. For our food aid service with monthly baskets, choosing the products isn’t always possible. This year, despite high demand, we received halal meat only twice, and at random times.”
Yitong nous conduit dans la salle de sto: Yitong takes us to the storage room. On the shelves, the products vary. We find various spices, from cumin to Afro-Creole spice blends, different types of rice, various beans, all kinds of nuts, and more.
« Avec Ma boîte à provisions, nous essay: “With Ma boîte à provisions, we try to meet the demands of the different communities. For example, the Haitian community expressed a great need for different types of beans. Likewise, the Latino community told us about its recurring need for corn flour. And it’s the same for the North African community, which asked us for wheat semolina.”
« Notre équipe est diversifiée, des memb: “Our team is diverse, from staff members to volunteers. That means we understand our communities’ culinary habits and can select the right ingredients. Take couscous, for example; we offer only one type, but that’s because the North African community, which is the main user among our clientele, prefers medium-sized grains. We add products based on the community’s requests.”
<strong>Mais comment réussissent-ils à a: But how do they manage to get a good price?
« Notre équipe se compose de moi, Kathle: “Our team is made up of me, Kathleen Phaëton, and Mame Bigué Dieng. We’re actively involved in negotiating prices with suppliers. Since we’re a community initiative, we’re not looking to make a profit, and we bypass intermediaries like the big supermarkets. We go after better prices.”
Malgré leurs efforts, Yitong doit reconn: Despite their efforts, Yitong has to admit that inflation is winning out over her negotiating talent. “We can’t offer products as simple as mayonnaise anymore; the quantity-to-price ratio is too unfavourable.”
Kathleen Phaëton, la coordonnatrice de l: Kathleen Phaëton, the Carrefour’s food security coordinator, explains the role of collaboration in the success of Ma boîte à provisions.
« Grâce au financement Projet impact col: “Thanks to funding from the Projet impact collectif with Centraide, we can carry out several projects in our neighbourhood.”
« Dans les produits proposés par Ma boît: “Among the products offered by Ma boîte à provisions, we include a component dedicated to food processing. So not only do we use unsold leftovers to prepare meals, but we also have partners like Les Jumeleurs and Mon Resto Saint-Michel, who prepare quality frozen meals at affordable prices, ranging from $3.85 to $5.50.”
De plus, Ma boîte à provisions a aussi u: In addition, Ma boîte à provisions also has a production component with urban agriculture. “We receive a number of foods from the <l1>Jardin des Patriotes</l1> and from the greenhouse at Louis-Joseph-Papineau high school. For example, the foods we sell come directly from the fall harvest in the garden. My colleagues who look after the garden have started planting exotic species like hibiscus. It’s not a product we sell yet, but we’ll surely have it next year, as we do with herbs.”
« Notre circuit-court d’approvisionnemen: “Our short supply and food processing chain is fully rooted in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood, fostering a direct connection between local producers and consumers, while encouraging a sustainable approach,” concludes Kathleen Phaëton.
De plus, La Converse a effectué des anal: In addition, La Converse carried out comparative analyses of supermarket receipts and Ma boîte à provisions receipts. With the exception of a few products, Ma boîte à provisions manages to reduce the total cost of the grocery bill.
Décembre tire à sa fin, et la nouvelle a: December is drawing to a close, and the new year promises new challenges. According to both food banks, cases like Mohamed’s will keep increasing, especially with overwhelming inflation. Food banks are trying to adapt to the needs of their clientele and, above all, to their culinary culture, but to do so, they need to be given resources that match the task. In the meantime, the Carrefour Populaire de Saint-Michel will be closed so the team can rest and regain their strength. The Centre d’entraide aux familles remains open, even over the holiday season.
